[b]Research on the Underworld[/b]

The research began quietly, as such things often did. A small team of investigative academics from the University of Kingsmount, sponsored by a private grant from the Institute of Social Studies, announced their intention to study organized crime in the Commonwealth of High Albany. Their focus, they claimed, was historical: an exploration of how the nations criminal underworld had evolved alongside its economic and political transformations. The announcement was covered in passing by a handful of newspapers, met with neither excitement nor outrage. A handful of public officials commented on the project with idle curiosity, while others dismissed it outright, uninterested in what was seen as an academic exercise with no practical consequence. The researchers, mostly professors and graduate students, planned to conduct interviews, examine old legal documents, and trace financial records.

Their work began in the archives, unearthing century-old records of smuggling rings, prohibition-era black markets, and the quiet disappearances of certain government informants. They scoured trade manifests from the 18th century, noting the anomaliesshipments that arrived with fewer goods than recorded, or mysteriously overvalued commodities moving through key ports. They studied transcripts of long-forgotten trials where men with too much influence walked free despite damning evidence. What they uncovered was less surprising than the clarity with which it all fit together. There was, undeniably, a patternone that stretched back beyond the Industrial Revolution, beyond the Colonial Age, into the earliest days of Albanys formation. A system, old as the nation itself, where crime did not simply coexist with governance but, in many ways, had become an extension of it.

At first, their findings drew little attention. There were no accusations, no grand theories of conspiracyjust historical observations. The researchers noted the peculiar tendency of criminal syndicates to shift operations whenever law enforcement grew too interested, how entire industries seemed to be quietly sustained by illicit funds, and how government projects, often underfunded on paper, found financial backing from untraceable sources. They noted the existence of the so-called Accord, a long-rumored understanding among criminals operating within Albanys borders: do not threaten the state, and the state will, in turn, not bring its full weight upon you.

The Accord, as the researchers traced it, had evolved from what was once a gentlemans agreement between smugglers and corrupt officials in the 17th century. By the Industrial Age, it had transformed into a structured, if unwritten, arrangement: organized crime could operate so long as it contributed to the economy and avoided disrupting internal stability. The Tithe was an open secretthe unspoken rule that for every ten crimes committed, at least two must benefit the state in some way. Sometimes, this meant direct financial contributions to government projects. Other times, it meant quietly dealing with foreign threats in ways official channels could not.

As the research progressed, the team ventured beyond old documents and court transcripts. They sought to speak with those who worked in the shadows. Through intermediaries, they reached out to retired smugglers, former law enforcement officials, and businessmen whose fortunes had suspicious origins. A few agreed to speakanonymously, always cautiously. The Committee, they were told, was real. Not a single organization, but a loose collection of the most powerful figures in the underworld, ever-changing but bound together by one unshakable principle: survival through order. The Committee ensured the Accord remained intact, maintaining the delicate balance between crime and state.

The government, it seemed, had long since learned that outright suppression of organized crime was impossible. Instead, it managed it, regulating it in ways that could never be publicly acknowledged. There were no extradition treaties with Albany, a fact that made the nation an ideal refuge for crime bosses worldwide. But even those who sought shelter within its borders were not free from consequence. The government retained the quiet power to seize assets, a tool used sparingly but effectively, ensuring that even the most untouchable figures remained tethered to the state's interests. The Committee itself was not immune to these pressures. While it wielded significant influence, it existed at the pleasure of the state, and any attempt to disrupt the established balance was met with swift correctionif not by officials, then by rival criminal elements eager to use government displeasure as an excuse for retribution.

As the research team compiled its findings, they found themselves met with increasing resistance. Archival requests were delayed or denied without explanation. Some of the older records they had previously accessed were suddenly classified. Individuals who had agreed to be interviewed rescinded their participation, citing personal concerns. The press, once mildly curious about their project, lost interest. Few newspapers ran follow-up stories, and those that did framed the research as speculative, even misguided.

Then, the warnings came. At first, they were subtle. A researcher returned to his office to find his desk rearrangednothing stolen, but everything slightly out of place. Another found her home address posted on an anonymous online forum. A third received a simple, unsigned letter: Some things are best left in the past.

The university administration, sensing the growing tension, withdrew its support, citing budgetary concerns. The Institute of Social Studies, which had originally funded the project, quietly revoked its grant. The lead researcher, a professor with decades of tenure, announced his resignation within the month, citing personal reasons. The graduate students who had assisted him dispersed, their names fading from the public record. No one was arrested. No charges were filed. It was as if the project had never existed.

And so, the research into Albanys criminal underworld ended as so many things did in the Commonwealthwithout fanfare, without scandal, without trace. Those who had followed the investigation closely understood what had happened. The Committee had watched, had waited, and had decided that the research had gone far enough. The government, either complicit or simply pragmatic, had ensured that no further questions would be asked.
[/spoiler]

[b]The suicide ship[/b]
A Sal-Baliz supply ship is sailing through the Argot-Shamat sea towards a port in [nation]Goleornacha[/nation].

Sir, Hydronian ship incoming! Dead ahead! shouted the captain of the ship, Abdul.
We cant compromise the supplies! Turn us around! Replied a Sal-Baliz leader called Ayub.
Yes sir! Replied Abdul. The ship began to turn around. The Hydronian Naval ship began to speed towards them. The Sal-Baliz ship was carrying bombs so it was imperative that the Hydronians didnt capture them, or worse, destroy them.
Fire the guns! Shouted Ayub. Around 20 Sal-Baliz fighters began firing AK47 rifles at the Hydronian Ship. It was a futile attempt. As the Hydronian ship approached, Ayub had to make a decision. Light the bombs! He shouted. The fighters were visibly confused. You heard me, LIGHT THE BOMBS!. They did as he asked. He was going to attempt to blow up the ship, and the Hydronians with it.

*BOOOOOM*. The back of the ship was gone. It began to sink, but there was nobody left alive to save it. Fortunately, the Hydronians were too far behind them to sustain any serious damage. A few minor injuries from the shockwave, but nothing more.
